nameStory: Wood Whitlow-grass gets its name from its woodland habitat and its historical use in folk medicine to treat whitlows - painful infections around fingernails and toenails. The 'grass' part is misleading since this is actually a member of the mustard family, but many small plants were simply called 'grass' in old naming traditions.
description: Wood Whitlow-grass is a tiny annual wildflower that's easily overlooked in New England's forests. This delicate plant grows just 2-6 inches tall with a small cluster of white flowers at the top. It's one of our earliest spring bloomers, appearing when most other plants are still sleeping. Despite being called a grass, it's actually related to mustard and cabbage plants.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers with four petals arranged in a cross shape, clustered at the top of slender stems. Each flower is only about 1/8 inch across and feels papery to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves covered in soft, star-shaped hairs that make them feel fuzzy or velvety. Most leaves cluster at the base of the plant with just a few tiny ones on the stem.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Extremely small and delicate, forming tiny rosettes close to the ground. The whole plant could fit in your palm and often grows in small patches.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, oval seed pods called siliques that split open when ripe. The pods are flattened and contain several tiny seeds.

habitat: Wood Whitlow-grass prefers moist, shaded areas in deciduous and mixed forests, often growing on rich, organic soil. Look for it along woodland paths, in forest clearings, or near stream banks where the soil stays consistently moist. It's extremely rare in New England, with only one confirmed observation.

seasonality.spring: Blooms very early in spring, often in April when snow may still be present. The tiny white flowers appear before most tree leaves emerge, taking advantage of the bright forest floor.
seasonality.summer: By early summer, the plant has usually completed its life cycle, setting seed and dying back. Look for dried stems and empty seed pods.
seasonality.fall: No visible presence above ground as this annual plant completes its life cycle in spring.
seasonality.winter: Seeds lie dormant in the soil, waiting for spring warmth to germinate into new plants.

funFact: Wood Whitlow-grass is so rare in New England that it's been documented only once in the entire region - making anyone who finds it a true botanical detective discovering one of our rarest wildflowers!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with Common Whitlow-grass, but Wood Whitlow-grass has more leaves on its stem and grows in forest habitats rather than open, disturbed areas. The fuzzy, star-shaped hairs on the leaves are also more prominent than on its common cousin.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - this isn't a grass at all! Like many old plant names, 'grass' was used for any small, inconspicuous plant. The whitlow connection comes from medieval herbalism, though there's no scientific evidence it actually treated nail infections.
compareHints: Wood Whitlow-grass differs from Common Whitlow-grass by having more stem leaves and preferring shaded forest habitats instead of sunny, disturbed ground. It's also much rarer and blooms slightly later in spring. Rock whitlow-mustard grows in completely different rocky, alpine conditions and has a more robust appearance.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common whitlowgrass differs from its relatives rock whitlow-mustard and wood whitlow-grass primarily by its habitat preferences and timing.
Rock whitlow-mustard differs from common whitlowgrass by its preference for rocky habitats (common whitlowgrass grows in disturbed soil and gardens) and its more robust, perennial-like appearance.
